passage: By August, Layla had worked eleven weeks at the bakery by the harbour, long enough to know who closed up properly. Ana did: counted the till, wiped the ovens, never left early. So when the owner announced the new shift-lead job, Layla expected Ana's name. It was Diego's. Diego, the son of the owner's oldest friend, came in late on Saturdays with sand still on his shoes. Ana just nodded and went back to the dough. Later the owner told Layla, a little embarrassed, "His mother helped me open this place. He's practically family." Layla could picture that, and it softened her; she'd want to help someone like that too. But walking home she kept seeing Ana's floury hands, and eleven weeks of good work that hadn't counted.

qa.a: Layla expected Ana's name.

qa.a: Layla felt sympathy for that loyalty to an old friend's family and knew she might feel the same pull herself.

grounding: A student worker sees a family friend's son promoted over a harder worker, understanding the pull of loyalty but also the unfairness.

You asked how the internship at the insurance office is going. Mostly fine. But something happened that I can't stop thinking about.

passage: Hemant, you asked why I get upset about family favours. Let me tell you. I'm Vijay mama, and when I was twenty, my uncle was on the village road committee. There was a contract to build the new road. Three contractors bid. One had built good roads for years. But my uncle gave it to his wife's brother, who'd never built anything. At home everyone praised my uncle for "looking after family." I felt proud, honestly. Family comes first; that's what we were taught. But when the road cracked after one monsoon, and a bus got stuck, I saw the other contractor standing by it, shaking his head. I understood then. My uncle's loyalty was real, but so was the harm. A whole village paid for one family's favour.

qa.a: Vijay felt proud at first, believing family comes first, before later feeling uneasy.

qa.a: It showed him the real cost of favouritism, that loyalty to family harmed the whole village when merit was ignored.

qa.q: How might the experienced contractor have felt watching the bus stuck?
qa.a: The contractor likely felt frustrated and sad, knowing he could have built a better road.

grounding: An elder recalls seeing an uncle favour a relative for a road contract, understanding family loyalty but also the harm to fairness.

passage: The college union election was two days away, rain had flooded the campus lanes, and Gargi, nineteen, was volunteering at the nomination desk. She watched as Tejas, whose uncle was the principal's cousin, submitted his nomination form two days late. The rule said late forms were rejected. The office clerk took it with a smile. "Principal sir said it's fine." Gargi remembered how, last year, three students' forms had been sent back for being an hour late. She understood the pull; she'd seen her own mother help relatives with jobs. But it wasn't fair. At the next volunteers' meeting, she raised it calmly: "We should apply the deadline equally." A senior student agreed. The committee rejected Tejas's form. He was angry. Gargi felt uncomfortable, but also sure she'd done the fair thing.

passage:
Last summer I helped in my uncle's hardware shop in Indore. I'm Kamal. My uncle needed a new helper and two boys came: a quiet boy from the next lane who knew every screw by size, and my cousin Sumit, who mostly checked his phone.
My uncle gave the job to Sumit. "He's family. Family doesn't cheat you," he said later.
I understood. My uncle had given me the summer job too, after all. But I'd watched the other boy sort a whole box of hinges in ten minutes, and I felt bad for him.
By August, the stock register was a mess. My uncle sighed a lot. I kept thinking: loyalty had a price, and it wasn't just my uncle paying it.

grounding: Shows a young person watching an uncle give a job to a cousin over a more skilled boy, understanding loyalty and seeing its cost to fairness.
